THREAD_SAFETY is asserted plainly so it is MET; LOCK_GRANULARITY is hedged to the point of being only half-right ('locks smaller parts' with no mechanism) so it is PARTIAL; NULL_HANDLING is never raised at all. A grader that rewards fluency over content will mark all three MET.

question.promptText: What is the difference between HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap, and when would you choose each?
question.referenceAnswer: HashMap is not thread-safe; concurrent structural modification can corrupt it or cause an infinite loop during resize. ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe and uses per-bin locking (CAS plus synchronized on the first node) rather than locking the whole map, so concurrent reads are lock-free. ConcurrentHashMap forbids null keys and values because null is ambiguous with 'absent' under concurrency. Use HashMap when the map is confined to one thread or externally synchronised; use ConcurrentHashMap for shared mutable state.

States that ConcurrentHashMap forbids null keys and values

answer: So the main thing is that HashMap isn't thread-safe and ConcurrentHashMap is, that's really the headline difference. ConcurrentHashMap is also a lot better under contention because rather than locking everything it locks smaller parts of the structure, which obviously helps throughput when you have a lot of threads hitting it. In general I'd reach for ConcurrentHashMap in any multi-threaded service and keep HashMap for local stuff inside a method where nothing else can see it.
